newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico risks import surge if VAT is cut - economists.
newsitem.headline: Mexico risks import surge if VAT is cut - economists.

text.p: Mexico could unleash a dangerous surge in imports and blow a hole in public finances if the government bows to political pressure for a cut in the value-added tax rate, economists said.

With the country just emerging from its bleakest recession since the 1930s, economists said a tax cut could contribute to consumer boom, similar to the one that helped precipitate Mexico's 1994-95 peso crisis.

"What I fear is that consumption will explode. If you reduce VAT, then we run the risk of a consumer boom, particularly in the second half of 1997 and the first half of 1998," said Rogelio Ramirez de la O, director of Mexico City-based economists Ecanal.
"Reducing VAT would be perverse. It would cause a highly undesirable outcome even if it seems high time for relief to family incomes," he said.

Opposition politicians, spurred by historic gains in the July 6 midterm elections, are mustering their forces for an assault on Mexico's ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) when the new Congress convenes at the start of September.
The VAT tax -- emblematic of what the PRI's opponents say is the party's distance from the concerns of ordinary people -- may emerge as the first big battleground issue.

Popular pressure is mounting for cutting VAT -- a tax on retail sales -- to 10 percent from the current 15 percent. Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz on Monday was heckled with calls of "Down with VAT" when he left a dance performance in the southern state of Oaxaca.

While the PRI and its opponents spar in the press, few have come up with concrete calculations on what such a tax cut would mean for Mexico's economy -- where green shoots of recovery are only just starting to appear.

Slowing inflation, increasing employment, recovering wages and a seemingly unstoppable peso have underpinned a 34.6 percent rise in consumer imports in May. That has put consumption back on the economic radar screen, Ramirez said.
Ramirez warned that consumption could rise too fast and said cutting VAT would run counter to policies to promote savings and protect Mexico against foreign capital volatility.
"Mexico is like a patient that has to recover carefully. It can't suddenly do strenuous exercise," he said.
Ortiz has said lopping five percent off VAT would blow a 25 billion peso hole in the budget, while attempts to recover the revenue by raising taxes elsewhere would fall short.
Salvador Kalifa, Monterrey-based financial and economic consultant, agreed in a newspaper column that cutting VAT would throw government finances off balance.
"I have no doubt that if we apply popular arithmetic which supports cutting VAT, we will end up taking in fewer pesos (in tax receipts) and saving only centavos," he said.

Economists said that although VAT receipts have exceeded forecasts -- up 13 percent in the second quarter of 1997 -- federal finances will come under greater pressure in the second half when new private pension plans get under way.
Mexico may therefore be less able to sustain a cut in government revenues that cutting VAT would entail, they said.
